extracted.intended_audience: graduate students and advanced undergraduates studying algebraic geometry (Math 216 readers)
extracted.subtask_description: Standards, theorems, and useful criteria about Čech cohomology, vanishing theorems, base change, Künneth, Riemann–Roch, degree, nefness, and Serre duality for quasicoherent/coherent sheaves on schemes (especially projective k-schemes and curves).

rubrics_metrics.name: Independence of Čech cohomology on choice of finite cover
rubrics_metrics.description: Our standing assumption is that X is quasicompact and separated. Hi_U(X,F) is independent of the choice of (finite) cover {Ui}. Precisely, for any two covers {Ui} and {Vi}, the maps Hi_{ {Ui} }(X,F) → Hi_{ {Vi} }(X,F) induced by the natural map of Čech complexes are isomorphisms. Define the Čech cohomology group Hi(X,F) to be this group.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the natural map of Čech complexes (18.2.1.1). The proof reduces to the case where one cover has one extra open set; use the short exact sequence of complexes (18.2.3.1) and the long exact sequence in cohomology. Check compatibility of restriction/localization maps and connecting homomorphisms with localization first.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quasiisomorphism viewpoint
rubrics_metrics.description: Maps of complexes inducing isomorphisms on cohomology groups are called quasiisomorphisms; the Čech construction yields a finer invariant (an element of the derived category of A-modules).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For experts: think in derived-category terms — quasiisomorphism class of the Čech complex is the invariant rather than just its cohomology groups.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compatibility with localization
rubrics_metrics.description: Maps such as Hi(F)_U → Hi(G)_U given by covariance 'commute with localization', and the connecting homomorphisms do as well; use this to identify localized long exact sequences with long exact sequences for the restricted cover on X_f = π^{-1}(D(f)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: First check that covariant maps commute with localization, then check connecting homomorphisms; this allows reduction to affine local computations by localizing at functions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Higher Čech cohomology vanishes on affine schemes
rubrics_metrics.description: The higher Čech cohomology Hi_U(X,F) of an affine A-scheme X vanishes for i > 0, for any affine cover U and quasicoherent F (Theorem 18.2.4).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Serre's argument is described as a partition-of-unity trick. Prove exactness of the extended Čech complex (global sections appended) (18.2.4.1); reduce to the case where one Ui = X (use short exact sequence (18.2.4.2)) or localize to distinguished opens D(f_i) so that each is contained in some affine Ui.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exactness of sequences of sheaves may be checked locally
rubrics_metrics.description: To show exactness of a sequence of sheaves it suffices to check exactness after localizing to a cover of distinguished opens D(f_i) with (f1,...,fr)=1.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use that exactness of sheaves is a local property and that quasicoherent sheaves localize as modules: Γ(Spec A, F)_f = Γ(Spec(A_f), F).

rubrics_metrics.name: Čech complex terminates at the number of affine opens
rubrics_metrics.description: If X is covered by n affine open sets, use these as the cover U, and the Čech complex ends by the nth step (property (vi)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hence when covering a scheme by n affines, cohomology beyond degree n vanishes for quasicoherent sheaves computed via that cover.

rubrics_metrics.name: Affine morphism pushforward preserves cohomology (pullback/pushforward compatibility)
rubrics_metrics.description: If π : X → Y is an affine morphism and Y is quasicompact and separated, then for a quasicoherent sheaf F on X there is a natural isomorphism Hi(Y, π_*F) ≅ Hi(X,F) (Exercise 18.2.E).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compute cohomology using an affine cover U of Y; π^{-1}(U) is an affine cover of X, compare Čech complexes. Use that affine morphisms are quasicompact and separated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Natural morphism from cohomology of pushforward to cohomology of source
rubrics_metrics.description: For any quasicompact separated morphism π : X → Y (with Y quasicompact separated) and F quasicoherent on X, there is a natural morphism Hi(Y, π_*F) → Hi(X,F) extending the map on global sections Γ(Y, π_*F)→Γ(X,F). This map is an isomorphism for i = 0 but need not be for higher i (Exercise 18.2.F).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware of counterexamples (e.g., i=1, X = P^1_k, F = O(-2), Y a point). Use this morphism when investigating pushforward cohomology but do not assume higher isomorphisms without hypotheses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Filtered colimits are exact on modules (cohomology and filtered colimits)
rubrics_metrics.description: In the category of modules over a ring, taking the colimit over a filtered set is an exact functor (reference 1.6.12).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this fact when proving statements about cohomology commuting with direct limits or inductive systems; it's often used to pass to limits in cohomology arguments (Exercise 18.2.G hints).

rubrics_metrics.name: Base change for cohomology under field extension (flat base change for fields)
rubrics_metrics.description: If X is a quasicompact separated k-scheme and F is coherent, then for any field extension K/k there is an isomorphism Hi(X,F) ⊗_k K ≅ Hi(X×_{Spec k} Spec K, F⊗_k K) for all i (Exercise 18.2.H).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For i=0 the result holds without quasicompact/separated hypotheses. More generally the statement generalizes to flat ring maps B←A with appropriate hypotheses (use flatness and quasicoherence). Useful for relating schemes over k to algebraically closed base fields.

rubrics_metrics.name: Base-point-freeness preserved by extension of base field
rubrics_metrics.description: If X is a scheme over k, L an invertible sheaf, and K/k a field extension, then L is base-point-free iff its pullback L_{k⊗K} on X×_k Spec K is base-point-free (Exercise 18.2.I).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Exercise 18.2.H with i=0 to compare spaces of sections; a basis of sections over k remains a basis after tensoring with K.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dimensional vanishing theorem
rubrics_metrics.description: If X is a projective k-scheme and F a quasicoherent sheaf on X, then Hi(X,F) = 0 for i > dim X (Theorem 18.2.6). More generally for Noetherian topological spaces and any sheaf of abelian groups, Hi(X,F) = 0 for i > dim X (Grothendieck).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The projective case is proved by covering X by dim X + 1 affines (using effective Cartier divisors on PN). For broader generality see derived functor methods (Chapter 23) and references [GrS],[Ha1].

rubrics_metrics.name: Künneth formula for cohomology of tensor products
rubrics_metrics.description: For quasicompact separated k-schemes X and Y and quasicoherent sheaves F on X and G on Y, we have H^m(X×_k Y, F ⊠ G) ≅ ⊕_{p+q=m} H^p(X,F) ⊗_k H^q(Y,G) (18.2.8).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof: choose affine covers of X and Y, form Čech complexes, identify the Čech complex of F⊠G with the total complex (tensor product) of the two Čech complexes, and use the Eilenberg–Zilber theorem to relate cohomology of tensor product of complexes to tensor products of cohomologies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cup product in Čech cohomology
rubrics_metrics.description: The cup product in Čech cohomology can be defined concretely (references: Liu Ex.2.17); a standard Čech description exists but is not needed here (18.2.9).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text notes an elegant description in Liu; keep in mind cup products are available in Čech theory for multiplicative structures on cohomology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cohomology of O(m) on projective space (interpretation of H^0 and H^n)
rubrics_metrics.description: H^0(P^n_A, O(m)) is interpreted as homogeneous degree m polynomials in x0,...,xn with A-coefficients. H^n(P^n_A, O(m)) is interpreted as homogeneous degree m Laurent polynomials where each xi appears with degree at most −1 (Remark 18.3.1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compute via the standard affine cover Ui = D(x_i) and the Čech complex (displayed in (18.3.2.1)-(18.3.2.2)); study exactness monomial-by-monomial by cases on negative exponents to prove Theorem 18.1.3 for P^n.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method: multidegree case analysis for Čech exactness on P^n
rubrics_metrics.description: When analyzing the Čech complex for O(m) on P^n, exactness can be checked by multidegree (degree in each xi), breaking into cases by how many exponents are negative (0,1,2,...), with explicit short exact sequences showing exactness in each case (18.3.2.3).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This reduces complicated global exactness to combinatorial/monomial checks; use mapping-cone or long exact sequence arguments to handle middle cases via top/bottom rows.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and usefulness of Euler characteristic
rubrics_metrics.description: For a projective k-scheme X and coherent F, hi(X,F) := dim_k Hi(X,F) finite, and χ(X,F) := Σ_{i=0}^{dim X} (−1)^i hi(X,F). Euler characteristics behave well (polynomial in parameters, additive in exact sequences) and are often easier to compute than individual cohomology groups.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use additivity: χ is additive in short exact sequences (Exercise 18.4.A); combine with vanishing theorems to deduce individual hi from χ.

rubrics_metrics.name: Riemann–Roch for line bundles on a regular projective curve
rubrics_metrics.description: For a divisor D on a regular projective curve C over a field k, χ(C, O_C(D)) = deg D + χ(C, O_C) (Essential Exercise 18.4.B).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prove by induction on |deg D| using the closed subscheme exact sequence and additivity of χ; every invertible sheaf is O_C(D). The usual reformulation: h^0(C,L) - h^1(C,L) = deg L - p_a(C) + 1.

rubrics_metrics.name: Degree of a line bundle via Euler characteristic
rubrics_metrics.description: Define deg L := χ(C,L) − χ(C,O_C) for an invertible sheaf L on a regular projective curve C; this equals the degree of the divisor of any nonzero rational section of L (Important Exercise 18.4.C).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This gives a cohomological definition of degree and matches classical counting of zeros and poles for rational sections. Use to prove functoriality of degree under pushforward and tensor product.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rank and degree for coherent sheaves on curves; additivity
rubrics_metrics.description: For a coherent sheaf F on an irreducible projective curve C, rank F is its rank at the generic point; define deg F = χ(C,F) − (rank F) χ(C,O_C) (18.4.4.1). Rank and degree are additive in short exact sequences (Exercises 18.4.H and 18.4.I).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Localize at generic point to compute rank; use additivity of χ to deduce additivity of degree. For vector bundles, degree equals degree of determinant bundle (Exercise 18.4.J).

rubrics_metrics.name: Arithmetic genus
rubrics_metrics.description: Arithmetic genus of a scheme X is defined as p_a(X) := 1 − χ(X, O_X). For integral projective curves over an algebraically closed field, p_a(X) = h^1(X, O_X).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use p_a in Riemann–Roch formulas for curves. For complex smooth projective curves, p_a equals the topological genus g (Miracle 18.4.3).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of degree to obstruct rational sections (example: universal plane conic)
rubrics_metrics.description: Degree computations can show nonexistence of rational sections: e.g., the universal plane conic family over P^5 has no rational section because intersection multiplicity/parity arguments show contradictions (Exercises 18.4.M–18.4.P).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Translate a hypothetical rational section into a divisor meeting fibers with multiplicity 1; use parity information from degrees on fibers to derive contradiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Length of a module and composition series (foundation for nonreduced Riemann–Roch)
rubrics_metrics.description: Length ℓ(M) is the length of the longest strictly increasing chain of submodules. Composition series subquotients are simple, and any two composition series have the same length (18.4.7–18.4.Q). Over a Noetherian local ring, finite length ⇔ m^n M = 0 for some n (18.4.R).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use length when working with sheaves supported on nonreduced components; length behaves like dimension for finite modules and is used in Riemann–Roch for nonreduced curves.

rubrics_metrics.name: Riemann–Roch for nonreduced curves
rubrics_metrics.description: For a projective curve C (possibly nonreduced) and coherent F, χ(L⊗F) − χ(F) equals the sum over irreducible components C_i of deg_L(C_i) times the length of F at the generic point η_i of C_i (Exercise 18.4.S).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reduce to the reduced case by filtrations via the nilpotent ideal sheaf; write L as tensor of O(n_i p_i) avoiding associated points of F and proceed by induction on the number of points.

rubrics_metrics.name: Numerical equivalence, Pic_τ, N1(X), and nefness
rubrics_metrics.description: Define deg_C L := deg_C i^*L for one-dimensional closed subschemes i:C ↪ X. L is numerically trivial if deg_C L = 0 for all integral curves C. Numerically trivial line bundles form Pic_τ X; N1(X) := Pic X / Pic_τ X. L is nef (numerically effective) if deg_C L ≥ 0 for all integral curves C. The nef Q-line bundles form a closed cone (nef cone) in N1_Q(X) (18.4.9–18.4.W).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Properties: nefness and numerical triviality are preserved under pullback by proper morphisms and under restriction to components; tensor and dual preserve numerical properties; ample bundles are nef; ampleness can be detected numerically (Kleiman's criterion).

rubrics_metrics.name: Picard number and finiteness (Néron–Severi remarks)
rubrics_metrics.description: The group N1(X) (Pic modulo numerically trivial) is a finitely generated free Z-module; its rank ρ(X) (Picard number) is finite. Over C one can show finiteness of ρ(X) by embedding into H^2(X,Z) (18.4.10–18.4.U).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a deep finiteness fact (Néron–Severi Theorem); use Hodge-theoretic/topological arguments over C for a simpler proof. Picard number appears in intersection-theoretic results such as the Hodge Index Theorem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Serre duality for smooth projective varieties
rubrics_metrics.description: If X is geometrically irreducible smooth projective k-variety of dimension n, there is an invertible sheaf ω_X such that h^i(X,F) = h^{n-i}(X, ω_X ⊗ F^∨) for all finite-rank locally free F, and a perfect pairing Hi(X,F) × H^{n-i}(X, ω_X ⊗ F^∨) → H^n(X, ω_X) ≅ k (Theorem 18.5.1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ω_X is a dualizing sheaf (and for smooth varieties equals the canonical bundle/determinant of the cotangent bundle). Serre duality is a cornerstone for Riemann–Roch and duality arguments but is more difficult to prove; it yields dimension-symmetry of cohomology groups.

rubrics_metrics.name: Canonical sheaf as dualizing sheaf for smooth varieties
rubrics_metrics.description: For smooth projective varieties, the invertible sheaf ω_X coincides with the canonical sheaf/determinant of the cotangent bundle Ω_{X/k} (18.5.2).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This identification links algebraic duality to the geometric notion of volume forms; its formal justification appears later (Chapter 30) and is important for explicit Serre duality computations.
